title: Estimators on the spot
objectives: Derive a quick estimator with its bias and variance at a whiteboard.

screens.title: The largest of nine
screens.prose: This lesson takes about 35 minutes, three minutes a question; say your reasoning aloud first. Nine draws are uniform on 0 to an unknown cap $\theta$. We set $\theta = 10$ and record the largest draw. Run the trials and watch the mean.

state.caption: Nine draws on 0 to 10. Run the trials.

screens.question: On average, how large is the largest of nine draws?

hints.text: Run 1,000 trials and read the mean line.
Nine draws cut $[0, 10]$ into ten gaps of equal expected size.
So the largest sits one gap below 10.

feedback.correct: 9: the largest draw falls short of the cap by 1 on average.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run the trials and read the mean.

byKey.cap: You assumed the largest draw reaches the cap. It never can, so on average it falls short.
byKey.one: 5 is the mean of one draw. The largest of nine sits much higher.

explain.text: On average the largest draw is $n\theta/(n + 1) = 9$. It undershoots by 1, so its bias is $-1$. The simulated mean converges to 9.

canvas.caption: After 1,000 trials the mean is close to 9.

screens.title: Undo the shortfall
screens.prose: Scaling by $(n + 1)/n$ removes the bias: $E\left[\tfrac{n+1}{n}M\right] = \theta$, where $M$ is the largest draw. A new sample of nine has largest draw 7.2.
screens.question: What is the unbiased estimate of $\theta$?

hints.text: Scale the largest draw, do not shift it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the largest draw by $10/9$.

byKey.plugin: You reported the largest draw itself. It is biased low, so scale it up by $10/9$.
byKey.down: You scaled by $9/10$. The largest draw falls short, so scale up by $10/9$.
byKey.add: You added 1, the shortfall when $\theta = 10$. The shortfall is a share of $\theta$, so multiply instead.

explain.text: $7.2 \times 10/9 = 8.0$. The fix multiplies, because the shortfall is a share of $\theta$, not a fixed amount.

screens.title: Compare the errors
screens.prose: With $\theta = 10$ and $n = 9$, the largest draw has variance $n\theta^2/((n + 1)^2(n + 2)) = 0.8182$. The fix has variance $\theta^2/(n(n + 2)) = 1.0101$. One uniform draw has variance $\theta^2/12$.

state.caption: Twice the mean is unbiased; its variance is still to find.

screens.question: Fill in the two missing figures.

hints.text: MSE is bias squared plus variance.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square the bias before adding, and scale the variance of a mean by 4.

byKey.r0c1: MSE adds the squared bias, $(-1)^2 = 1$, to the variance 0.8182.

explain.text: The largest draw has MSE $1 + 0.8182 = 1.8182$; the fix has 1.0101. Twice the mean is unbiased, but its variance is $100/27 = 3.7037$. The largest draw carries most of the information about the cap.

screens.title: Unbiased is not best
screens.prose: Normal data, $n = 10$, $\sigma^2 = 1$. We divide the sum of squared deviations by $d$. A candidate says $d = 9$ wins because it is unbiased. Estimation lesson l4-bias-against-variance did this slowly for $n = 5$.

state.caption: Bias in units of $\sigma^2$; variance and MSE in units of $\sigma^4$.

screens.question: Which divisor gives the smallest mean squared error?

options.why: You chose the unbiased divisor. Its variance, 0.2222, is the largest of the three, and so is its MSE.
Dividing by $n$ gives 0.19, better than 9 but not the best.

hints.text: Add the squared bias to the variance on each row.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fill the MSE column: bias squared plus variance.

byKey.nine: You chose the unbiased divisor. Zero bias, but the largest variance: MSE 0.2222.

explain.text: MSE is bias squared plus variance: 0.2222, 0.19 and 0.1818. Dividing by $n + 1 = 11$ wins, because a little bias buys a larger fall in variance. Say it in one sentence: unbiased is not the same as best.

screens.title: Shrink a coin
screens.prose: A coin is flipped 10 times and shows $k$ heads. Compare $k/n$ with the shrunk $(k + 1)/(n + 2)$. The bars show each one's MSE as you slide the true $p$.
screens.question: Shrinking helps for $p$ in a middle band. Where is the upper end of that band?

hints.text: Slide $p$ up from 0.5 and watch the bars.
Shrinking adds a bias of $(1 - 2p)/12$, which grows away from the middle.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where the two bars are equal above $p = 0.5$.

byKey.half: At $p = 0.5$ shrinking helps most. Slide upwards until the two bars swap.
byKey.one: Near $p = 1$ shrinking hurts: it pulls ten heads in ten down to $11/12$.

explain.text: At $p = 0.5$ the MSEs are 0.0174 against 0.025, so shrinking helps. Its bias grows towards the ends, and the bars cross at $p = 0.862$ and 0.138. Shrinking helps near the middle and hurts far from it.

screens.title: A rate from waiting times
screens.prose: Five waiting times come from an exponential with rate $\lambda = 2$, so their mean is $1/2$. The plug-in estimate of the rate is $1/\bar x$. Run the trials.
screens.question: On average, what does $1/\bar x$ give?

hints.text: Run 1,000 trials and read the mean.

feedback.correct: 2.5: the plug-in rate is biased high.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run the trials and read the mean.

byKey.unb: $\bar x$ is unbiased for $1/\lambda$, but $1/\bar x$ is not unbiased for $\lambda$. Small means give huge rates.
byKey.mean: 0.5 is the mean waiting time. The question asks for the rate.

explain.text: $E[1/\bar x] = n\lambda/(n - 1) = 5 \times 2/4 = 2.5$, which the simulation approaches. Inverting an unbiased estimate breaks unbiasedness, because $1/x$ is convex. The fix is $(n - 1)/(n\bar x)$.

canvas.caption: After 1,000 trials the mean is near 2.5.

screens.title: Mean squared error
screens.prose: Each time we took the estimator's mean for the bias and its spread for the variance. $$\operatorname{MSE}(\hat\theta) = E[(\hat\theta - \theta)^2] = \operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta)^2 + \operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta).$$ Then we compared the totals. Say it aloud: bias squared plus variance.
screens.question: An estimator has bias 0.3 and variance 0.16. What is its MSE?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square the bias, then add the variance.

byKey.nosq: You added the bias without squaring it. Use $0.3^2 = 0.09$.
byKey.var: You gave the variance alone. Add the squared bias.

screens.title: Why the largest draw falls short
screens.prose: Put the whiteboard argument in order. One line does not belong.
screens.question: Order the steps that give $E[M] = n\theta/(n + 1)$.

lines.text: $P(M \le m) = (m/\theta)^n$ for $0 \le m \le \theta$: all $n$ draws must lie below $m$.
Differentiate: the density of $M$ is $n m^{n-1}/\theta^n$.
That is $n\theta/(n + 1)$, so the bias is $-\theta/(n + 1)$.
$P(M \le m) = nm/\theta$, since any of the $n$ draws can be the largest.
lines.why: That adds the $n$ chances. The largest is below $m$ only if every draw is, so multiply: $(m/\theta)^n$.

hints.text: When is the largest draw below $m$?
Every draw is below $m$, each with chance $m/\theta$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start with the chance that the largest is below $m$.

byKey.d1: You added the chances. Every draw must be below $m$, so multiply them.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line that belongs. Only one line is wrong.

explain.text: The largest is below $m$ only when every draw is, so its CDF is $(m/\theta)^n$. Its mean is $n\theta/(n + 1)$. For $n = 9$ and $\theta = 10$ that is 9.

screens.title: An auction cap
screens.prose: A desk sees nine auction clearing prices. It models them as uniform from £0 up to an unknown cap. The largest is £6.30.
screens.question: Using the largest price, what is the unbiased estimate of the cap?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the largest price by $10/9$.

byKey.plugin: You reported the largest price. It always falls short of the cap, so scale it up.
byKey.down: You scaled by $9/10$. Scale up by $10/9$.
byKey.mean2: Twice the mean, £9.42, is also unbiased, but its error is far larger. The question asks for the largest-price estimate.

explain.text: $6.30 \times 10/9 = 7.00$, so the cap is about £7.00. On average the largest price falls short of the cap by a tenth of the cap.

screens.title: The follow-up: which would you report
screens.prose: The interviewer asks: which estimate of the cap would you report, and why? The bars show each estimator's MSE when $\theta = 10$ and $n = 9$.
screens.question: Which answer would you give?

options.text: $(n + 1)/n$ times the largest: unbiased, and the lowest MSE, 1.01
The largest itself: it is the maximum likelihood estimate
options.why: It is the MLE, but it is biased low and its MSE is 1.82.

options.text: Twice the mean: it uses every draw
options.why: It uses every draw, yet its MSE is 3.70. The largest draw holds the information about the cap.

options.text: The largest itself: it never overshoots the cap
options.why: True, it never overshoots, but it always undershoots. That is a bias of $-1$.

hints.text: It also has the shortest bar.

feedback.correct: Report the scaled largest draw, with its reason.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Give the estimator with the lowest MSE, and say why.

byKey.mle: You picked the MLE. Name it, then say it is biased low, and scale it.

explain.text: Report $(n + 1)/n$ times the largest: it is unbiased and has the lowest MSE, 1.01. The plain largest is biased low, and twice the mean wastes information. Give the number and the reason in one breath.

ideas: Write the estimator, take its mean for the bias and its spread for the variance.
Compare estimators by MSE: bias squared plus variance.
Unbiased is not best: divide by $n + 1$ for normal data, and shrink a coin only near the middle.

formula.name: Mean squared error
formula.note: The largest of $n$ uniform draws has mean $n\theta/(n + 1)$.

summary.trap: The unbiased divisor $n - 1$ has the largest MSE of the three.

quiz.prose: Four draws are uniform on 0 to $\theta$. The largest is 8.
quiz.question: What is the unbiased estimate of $\theta$?

byKey.plugin: The largest draw is biased low. Scale it by $5/4$.
byKey.down: You scaled by $4/5$. Scale up instead.

quiz.question: Thirty normal draws. Which divisor of the sum of squared deviations gives the smallest MSE?

options.why: That is the unbiased divisor. Its variance is the largest of the three.
Dividing by $n$ beats 29, but $n + 1$ beats both.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. For normal data the best divisor is $n + 1$.

explain.text: For normal data the MSE is smallest at $d = n + 1 = 31$. The small bias is worth the fall in variance.

quiz.question: An estimator has bias $-0.2$ and variance 0.05. What is its MSE?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square the bias, then add the variance.

byKey.abs: You added the bias without squaring it.
byKey.var: You left out the squared bias.
byKey.neg: You added the bias as a signed number. Square it first.

quiz.question: What is the shrunk estimate $(k + 1)/(n + 2)$ of $p$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add one to $k$ and two to $n$.

byKey.plugin: You gave $k/n = 1$. The shrunk estimate is $4/5$.

explain.text: $(3 + 1)/(3 + 2) = 0.8$. Shrinking keeps a small sample from claiming certainty.
